subsubtopic: SUGGESTION MUNICIPALITIES PARTICIPATE IN PROCESS OF CONSTITUTIONAL REFORM-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Considering that the major socioeconomic change in Canada since 1867 has been industrialization and urbanization, that the majority of people of Canada are metropolitan dwellers and that the Science Council has estimated that 90 per cent of the Canadian population will live in an urban environment by the year 2000, that municipalities are required to provide an ever-increasing number of essential services to our population, and that municipal governments are closer to the people and provide more essential services to their respective populations than any other level of government, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Stormont-Dundas (Mr. Lumley):
That this House call upon provincial governments to invite the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities to participate in the ongoing process of constitutional reform with a view to entrenching powers in the constitution so as to provide municipalities with the powers and revenues necessary to permit them to effectively discharge their responsibilities and to provide the services expected of them by the Canadian public.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: MR. MCKINNON-VARIANCE IN ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Mr Speaker, my question is one of privilege. It affects all hon. members, but most particularly members of the opposition in that they ask more questions in the House than members opposite.
This question of privilege relates to an answer given to me by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) with supporting evidence given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and another answer which I received to a written question. The variance between the answers is such that it is quite apparent one or another of the answers is false.
To get to the evidence, Mr. Speaker, I received an answer to written question No. 649 from the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) or his representative. The question reads:
Privilege-Mr. McKinnon
Did Chancellor Schmidt personally or some of the other bidders ask for a few more months beyond the August 1 deadline to improve their bids on the new fighter aircraft contract, and, if so, which companies submitted additional proposals after August 1 ?
The answer to that question reads:
I am informed by the Department of External Affairs and National Defence as follows: No.
So the written reply was, "No, Chancellor Schmidt did not ask for an extension nor did any of the other companies." When I saw that answer I set about the necessary research to find written documentation of the opposite approach. May I now present two conflicting pieces of evidence, one from a press conference and one from Hansard.
First I quote from a transcript of the Prime Minister's press conference dated November 14, 1978 held in Ottawa. Mr. Jack Best asked a question of the Prime Minister concerning the new fighter aircraft and wanted to know, in view of the postponement of the contract process, how firm and total the government's commitment was to purchase. The Prime Minister answered as follows:
Completely firm and total. If there has been a slippage, it has been at the demand of those who are making bids. When I saw Chancellor Schmidt this summer, he had heard about our inclination to reduce the, I think, seven options to a smaller number and he personally, but this is true of some of the other bidders, asked for a few more months so that they could improve their bids. And, the Department of Defence in agreement with the government just felt that if the bids could be improved even in terms of off-sets to Canada, in terms of the number of planes which could be purchased for a given amount of money or in terms of their efficiency in the performance of certain tasks we would willingly give them a few more months.
As can be seen this is a direct contradiction of the written answer I have received. One must be false. Incidentally, the Prime Minister and Chancellor Schmidt conferred on July 16 and 17, 1978.
In the event a transcript is not enough evidence, I wish to draw Your Honour's attention to page 867 of Hansard dated November 7, 1978, where the Minister of National Defence, in answer to a question put by me concerning the new fighter aircraft, said:
As hon. members know, the vendors asked for additional time to submit, we have given them that additional time to submit-
Further along in his statement the minister said:
-if I may state the status now; there has been a deferment to give the vendors an opportunity to resubmit.
So the Prime Minister said yes, the companies, and Chancellor Schmidt personally, had asked for additional time. The Minister of Defence stated yes in the House of Commons.
Now in the House of Commons I have been informed that the answer is no. It is not easy, Mr. Speaker, to determine in this case who is responsible for the falsehood, but certainly there has been a falsehood, and it is my understanding that that means my privilege in this House, and indeed the privileges of all members, have been abused.
The precedent in a case such as this is fairly clear. The nineteenth edition of May's Parliamentary Practice states at page 141:

February 14, 1979
Privilege-Mr. McKinnon
It is a breach of privilege to present or cause to be presented to either House or to committees of either House, forged, falsified or fabricated documents with intent to deceive such House or committees or to subscribe the names of other persons or fictious names to documents intended to be presented to either House or to be privy to or cognizant of, such forgery or fraud.
I might say that the Chair used this citation in reaching a decision in the case raised before Christmas by my colleague, the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence), which confirmed that provision of false information to a member of parliament can be an infringement on his ability to carry out his duties. The reply to my question, signed by the parliamentary secretary, was obviously and demonstrably false, unless the statement by the Prime Minister at his press conference and the statement by the Minister of Defence at page 867 of Hansard were themselves fabrication.
It is difficult to believe that neither the Department of External Affairs nor the Department of National Defence was not aware of requests from bidders about which both the Prime Minister and Minister of Defence appeared to be completely knowledgeable. I wonder, therefore, what kind of process these written questions go through. Perhaps this answer I received reflects an attempt to mislead me by directly contradicting other information given publicly. Perhaps it reflects the incompetence of those providing the answers, or the impossibility of providing factual replies consistent with those given in the House. In this respect I would ask you to note the brevity of the reply.
We all realize that the government does not have to provide an answer to written questions, but if it does reply surely there is an obligation to make an honest effort to avoid deceptive or completely untrue responses.
In the ruling of December 6, the Chair asked:
Does that lead us to the conclusion that, by virtue of an act or omission, the House, or a member, has directly or indirectly been impeded in the performance of its functions or his duty, or that there has been a tendency to produce such a result? If I so find, then I really have no choice but to find, prima facie, that a contempt has been committed.
I believe in this case, sir, my attempts to follow up and ask questions about the fighter acquisition program have been impeded by the untruthful reply to one of my questions.
If you find I have a prima facie case of privilege, I would move:
That the reply to written question 648, containing an assertion demonstrably at variance with the facts as stated by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Defence, be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections for investigation and report.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, February 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Buchanan that Bill C-12, to amend the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act, the Public Service Superannuation Act, the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act and the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate on Bill C-12 not only because of its significance and importance to all of us, especially to those who have dedicated their lives to the public service, not only because I come from the metropolitan area of Dartmouth-Halifax where, next to Ottawa, we have perhaps the highest per capita share of public servants in the country, but for a particular reason. Within my constituency lies one of the largest military establishments in our country. It embraces many thousands of active members of the Canadian armed forces, as well as thousands who are living out their lives on pensions.
I enter the debate with mixed feelings. If the bill does represent a sincere and serious effort on the part of the government-and here I quote the words of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan)-"to firm up the financial underpinnings of the program to ensure we are not stirring up future trouble for taxpayers and public service pensioners" then perhaps it can be welcomed. Certainly it would be needed. There is very real concern abroad in the land with respect to the whole subject of indexation. Concern has been expressed both by the taxpayers and by the public servants.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext: You've made it.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I've made it. Somebody has taken my picture. It is disturbing to see a flash bulb go off. Perhaps it is because the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) is just leaving the chamber that we are celebrating by taking pictures. Anyway, the taxpayer feels that he or she will be left to pay for what has been described by some over-zealous partisans on this question as overly generous public service pensions. For his part, the public servant feels that protection against the ravages of inflation may now, or at some time in the future, be removed. As I see it, Bill C-12 was intended to dispel both these fears. Even more to the point, I believe the bill will destroy the basis upon which some of these fears have grown- the distortions which have been placed in front of us all. It strikes me that intrinsically this is what faces us.
What concerns me in any event is that the bill may merely represent another government exercise in "ad hockery" and camouflage. I am concerned because I suspect the government

does not know what it is going to do about indexation and is merely trying to buy time with the legislation which is before us. It may be that information available to the government and its actuaries and senior financial advisers is such that they cannot come to a firm decision at this time. What they have done on the eve of an election is to introduce a measure and let it proceed to a certain stage in the process of its becoming law, knowing well in their hearts and minds that nothing will be done about it until after the next general election.
I have been concerned for some ten or 12 years about the relationship of the government as an employer to its employees in the public service of Canada. On questions of pay and pensions perhaps it is time that the cabinet recognized that there is no longer a need for a direct relationship between the policy-making structure, the cabinet, and the employee. Perhaps it is time we began to examine the usefulness of an extended concept of the Treasury Board which allows it such authority and stature as to make it the employer, and not this parliament.
If we look to those areas of this country where there is a concentration of public servants, for whatever reason-perhaps it is the longevity of the present government; 15 or 16 years is perhaps too long for one group of individuals to lead effectively-we find that the majority of public servants are represented by members of this side of the chamber. I do not put that forward or postulate it as too serious a matter, but it seems to me that, given present circumstances and the lateness of our parliamentary mandate, perhaps none of us, including members of the government, has any right to be meddling with the affairs of those who serve the public in this country. We should not be dealing in an ad hoc manner with amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act or any of the seven or eight acts which affect directly or indirectly the careers of the public servants of this country, certainly not in the dying months, weeks or even days of an already tired parliament. I think the public servants of this country deserve something a little better than that.
I said that I am concerned that we might be dealing with this matter on an ad hoc basis. We do not have the answers to the questions of concern to my parliamentary colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander). There are literally dozens of questions with respect to this matter which need to be examined in depth. That is why my colleague said that we are prepared to let this matter go to committee where we can conduct the type of scrutiny and review which is required, and I hope that can be done today.
I have some fear about legislation which enables the government to appear to the taxpayer as if it is getting tough with the public service, and to the public service as if it is getting away with a good break. That seems to me to be the wrong way to approach the matter. Much more thought and study have to be given to the relationship between this institution and the employees of the Government of Canada. To have parliament regulating the relationship between employer and employee in
February 14, 1979

the 1970s and 1980s is wrong. We cannot do it efficiently. As I have suggested, I think we should look much more seriously at the extended concept of a treasury board, not only in fact but also in appearance, assuming the responsibilities of employer. We should look seriously at removing from this chamber control over the constant ups and downs which face every member of the public service when issues of this sensitivity come before us.
I do not want to deal at any great length with the specific content of this bill as it relates to the 200,000 or 300,000 public employees in the country, but I would like to make a few comments about a segment of the public service which I think needs some special recognition. I refer to members of the Canadian Armed Forces.
I remind hon. members of the unique position of members of the Canadian armed forces in our society. It is unique in the sense that they do not enjoy the privilege of freedom with respect to their tenure. In fact most of them are forced to retire. The vast majority of them are forced into retirement at age 55. Many are forced to retire at ages even younger than that. I am talking about a particular group of public employees in the military category, the pensions of these individuals as they are affected by unique circumstances, and the relationship they have with us.
Canadian forces annuities are paid by the Department of National Defence from either the old defence services pension continuation account or the Canadian forces superannuation account, not out of the usual public service funds. The average retirement age for Canadian forces personnel is significantly lower than for public servants generally. 1 bring to the attention of the House again the involuntary or statutory nature of retirement from the forces of armed forces personnel.
I am aware that some form of Treasury Board-DND committee was established a few years back to make representations on matters regarding personnel compensation, including pension concerns. One cannot be certain of what real input this committee has. I hope this will be dealt with when this bill comes before the appropriate committee.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) was in the chamber earlier today. Undoubtedly he is now out about his departmental responsibilities. I hope he will participate in this debate. The minister suggested snidely that the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) has been preoccupied with the question of privilege he raised this afternoon since the beginning of the year instead of asking questions about the military and the posturing of this government. I thought that to be beneath the minister and the usual attitude for parliament he displays. I thought the minister to be somewhat contemptuous. I wish he were here now so that I could say that to him. Very few have been as diligent in support of the Canadian military as has been the hon. member for Victoria.
While the minister makes comments and observations of the kind to which I referred, he does not bother to get on his feet to make a contribution on behalf of the 75,000 or 80,000 men and women in this country he represents and for whom he has a responsibility and obligation. I suggest to him, just as I
Pensions
would suggest to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen), that if he wants to enjoy the title of deputy prime minister he should get up in the House and speak to members if for no other reason than to recognize that a member has the right to be heard and that his constituents have the right to air their grievances. His attitude is typical of the government's attitude in the dying months of this government. This afternoon, the question of the security of those retiring from the public service of Canada, and the security of oil supplies for a major oil refinery process in Atlantic Canada drew from him not even an utterance. I know he must consider the question seriously, but, being Deputy Prime Minister he should keep himself advised and he should rise in the House and participate in the debate so that we will know what is going on.
I say the same thing to the Minister of National Defence. Where is he in this debate? Perhaps in what is left of the afternoon he will join us, and I hope he does. I hope the minister will not only address himself to the concerns of those serving in the forces, but also, either here or before the committee, personally or through his parliamentary secretary, will address himself to the concerns of those who have already retired. The minister will be aware that many of these people have been what you could only call long forgotten and neglected individuals.
There are 60,000 annuitants receiving Canadian forces pensions today. My own province of Nova Scotia has more Canadian forces pensioners per capita than any other province and, indeed, only Ontario and British Columbia have more actual service pensioners than Nova Scotia. However, I am sure that all hon. members, regardless of the constituencies they represent, are familiar with some of the difficulties which these individuals face. It is interesting to note that the average pension paid to ex-servicemen is approximately $3,400 a year. Even with full indexing, I do not think anyone should fear that these people are suddenly going to be living in the lap of luxury.
I enjoy listening to my colleagues. I listened with interest to my distinguished colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), when he voiced his concerns on this bill, and I agree with him. We should not only be talking about protection of income for public servants, the military and the RCMP; we should be talking about the extension of this principle to every Canadian, the right of these people to enjoy, as he so well stated it, not only protection against inflation but to enjoy with the rest of our society the increases in our standard of living.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I differ with him because I think only the private sector should provide the means to do it. I do not think that the assumption by government of the means of production would in fact satisfy that. But at least at the end we are on the same track. How can a pensioner receiving $3,400 a year cope on that? That is absolute poverty, not relative poverty. If you

February 14, 1979
Pensions
even gave him only 10 per cent, you are only giving him $340 a year-plus $30 a month-plus $1 a day. Will that put him in the lap of luxury? God knows, the old 85 rule was a cancer on our concern for our retired forces personnel. Now they have made it even worse.
At present less than 45 per cent of Canadian forces pensions are indexed in some form. However, this percentage will almost certainly decline with the removal of the 85 rule and the gradual raising of the indexing age from 55 to 60. To a certain extent I can understand and appreciate the rationale for this change. There is no doubt that present regulations encouraged early retirement and provided opportunities for abuse, to the extent that some former well-paid public servants are able to receive indexed pensions while drawing top salaries in the private sector at a relatively young age. But it is one thing to take away the option of early retirement with indexing for those who have the choice, and it is altogether different for those in the Canadian forces who are forced to retire at an early age. For these servicemen there is no option of serving beyond the age of 55, except in the rarest of circumstances.
It will mean that some servicemen will have to go as long as 20 years on a static pension, with inflation rising as high as 10 per cent per annum during some of those years. Now we have in front of us a step being taken, ostensibly for the purpose of inducing one group of public servants to remain employed beyond the age of 55. It will have a deleterious and serious effect on the serviceman who has been waiting patiently for the increase in his pension that would normally come at age 55. Now this is denied him. It seems to me that not only has the serviceman been under a specific disadvantage but he will be under an even greater disadvantage under the provisions of this bill. Very much the same special case can be put forward for members of the RCMP.
There are those who will argue that the early retirement age of Canadian forces personnel, voluntary or not, provides them with an opportunity to add significantly to their pension income by taking on a second career. However, this is more easily said than done. The Canadian forces long serving pensioners association claims that up to 75 per cent of ex-servicemen cannot find gainful or meaningful employment once they have retired. I strongly suspect this figure is even higher today, with the general economic slowdown and the high rate of unemployment. Even in the best of circumstances there are profound difficulties for an individual attempting to start a second career at the age of 45 or 50.
I am convinced that the serviceman, like the vast majority of other public servants, in no way wants to be viewed as a drain on the taxpayers of this country. He is more than willing to pay his fair share to a financially sound pension scheme. Indeed, this is what most forces personnel assumed they were doing when they elected to pay an additional contribution toward indexing under the 85 formula. We remember the afternoon when that was sneaked through when we were ostensibly recalled to debate a railway matter, and were told that while we are here we might as well do something else. This was some years ago.

As members of parliament we have a very strong responsibility, in dealing with this bill, to ensure that we lay a truly solid foundation which will guarantee some measure of protection for all public servants against the continually rising cost of living, but I suggest to hon. members that we have a particular responsibility to those who serve us within the parameter of a very strict and rigid discipline. We order the lives of members of the Canadian armed forces in virtually every way. We do the same with our national police force. We tell them under what circumstances they can enter, and precisely under what circumstances they will leave. We thrust, into an other than a sound economic environment, men who have unique training capabilities and capacities. We pay them an average of $3,400 or $3,500 a year in terms of pension. That is all they get on the average. It is very easy to find the exceptions, the $25,000 a year pensions in all sectors of the Canadian public service, but the average is only $3,400. As I say, we thrust them into the labour market in an unique era in our economic development when job opportunities are rare and jobs are difficult to come by, and we expect them to find gainful and meaningful employment. What do we do in the private sector with an expert on torpedoes? We have a very particular responsibility to our Canadian armed forces personnel on their retirement.
I am in complete disagreement with the provisions of this bill which extend indexing yet another five years to age 60. I regret the minister has seen fit to mix all of these pension matters in one omnibus bill. They should have been dealt with separately. They have unique characteristics, and we tend to downplay the importance of one or another because they are lumped together.
We welcome the opportunities which lie ahead in committee to pursue, with every bit of our energy and talent, the many, many questions before us. We welcome the opportunity to hear the concerns of all professional organizations which come before the committee. Also we welcome the opportunity to take a look at the several reports which are in existence and on which we must arrive at some conclusion.
I have very little reason to believe that the bill will ever become law prior to a general election. In that context I return to the camouflage and the ad hockery of this measure. I do not think the government wants to do anything at this point in time. The government believes it has captured the best of two worlds. In fact it has got the public thinking that the government has given the public service a good swift kick, and public servants think they are protected. In reality neither of those two situations exist. The government is uncertain of itself in this particular area. The matter has not been studied sufficiently. Perhaps we have no right at this time in the life of this parliament even to consider tinkering or playing around with the superannuation accounts.
When this matter is before the committee I hope the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) and the Minister of National Defence will encourage or send their parliamentary secretaries so that the ministers' views respecting members of the national
February 14, 1979

police force and Canadian armed forces can be made known to the members of the committee, and through them to the House, as well as to the members of the police force and the armed forces. I add that particular note to the remarks of my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West. In its consideration of these two particular aspects of the public service,
I urge the government not to overlook their uniqueness and the characteristics of their relationships with us. Also I urge the government to recognize the added responsibilities and difficulties which particularly members of the Canadian armed forces have when they attempt to obtain gainful and meaningful employment outside the services.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-12 because it affects many people in the upper Ottawa valley. I represent a large number of Crown employees at Atomic Energy of Canada, Ltd. in Chalk River, a large number of military personnel in one of the largest bases in Canada at Petawawa, and a large number of public servants in various departments located throughout the area.
We must remember that we have one of the best personally disciplined armed forces in the world. We have a lot of talent in the scientific field and in our public service generally. In the entire region of eastern Ontario which I represent, I appreciate and the region appreciates, what these people and these employment factors really mean to our over-all community. Without these people, our community would have to fall back on the timber trade, the limited number of factories that we have, and the commercial community, which latter of course would be much smaller.
During the last few years there have been many upsetting events throughout the world, not only of a military nature but certainly to a very large degree of an economic nature as well. Among these have been the uncertain conditions in the Middle East and the supply of energy to the western world. These uncertainties seem to be increasing as time goes on and, as a result, they have a very direct effect on the economies of western countries and inflationary trends. World conditions, along with the difficulties we have faced at home, have had far-reaching effects on many facets of our economic and social life. Bill C-12 is one example of how pressures have been brought to bear in one area of our domestic life as Canadians. There seems to be one assumption which we hear a great deal about today, that inflation is here to stay and everything will continue to rise for years to come.
Unsettled conditions in the past few years, and the unpredictable events which have happened in the world, have caused many problems for us and other nations. At the same time we must not rule out the possibility that certain events may lie ahead in the world picture today which can very well have a different effect on the economies of the western nations and, as a result, have a reverse effect on inflationary trends. For example, what will happen when the so-called third world countries become more self-supporting? What will happen
Pensions
when certain potential giants in the world today which are not highly industrialized become so in the immediate years ahead and goods and services become more available to all?
I was glad to hear the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan) and others in the House mention the past diatribes of the National Citizens' Coalition which seems to look upon the Canadian scene as its own personal domain, and which is trying to mold public opinion to suit its own purposes. The one thing which can be said about the National Citizens' Coalition is that one can realize readily its membership has not suffered very much by the inflationary trends of the past few years. Otherwise, they would not be able to produce the full-page newspaper ads and the other means they use to snowball the public. Perhaps they should be looking at their own various company pension plans and indexing in order to find out just how they are treating their own employees in this day and age. The fact that Bill C-12 places the various public pension plans discussed in the bill on a self-financing basis, automatically should withdraw it from such vindictive and unjustifiable comments.
As long as I have been around Parliament Hill I have never ceased to wonder why bills in the House cannot be written up in legal jargon on one side of the page and in layman's language on the other. I have a perfect example of what 1 mean before me at the present time. I have had many inquiries with regard to this bill from public servants, employees of Crown corporations and from members of the Canadian armed forces.
The question that keeps cropping up from the Canadian armed forces is, just where do they stand with the annual rate of inflation having regard to their pension at sixty years of age, if in fact they are required to retire, say, at the age of 44, 47 or 51 etc? The answer to that question is buried in the legal jargon found on page 7 of the bill starting at paragraph (b) of proposed section 4(1), sub-clauses (i) (ii) (iii) (iv) and (v). The latter sub-clause to be found at the top of page 8.
If a corporal retires at age 44, he will receive at age 60 the cumulative rate of inflation for the total 16 years, and his pension will go up accordingly at age 60. As for the immediate indexing of his pension, this does not come into question, because when he retires now he does not receive the indexing at the age of 44, and will not under this present legislation, so nothing has changed for his immediate future. But the fact that the indexing is cumulative for him during those 16 years means that his pension will, in fact, be worth something to him at age 60, in the event the inflationary rate continues.
For brigadier generals, who are classified as general service, they will retire at age 55 so this bill will affect those who are retiring immediately or in the next few years. A general who is classified as, say a specialist, such as a chaplain, dentist, legal, medical, music, nursing, or personnel development, have a compulsory release age of 60, and generals who have reached that position by virtue of being commissioned from the ranks have a compulsory release at age 55. A full colonel in the

February 14, 1979
Pensions
general service retires at the age of 55. A colonel under the specialist title must retire at 58, and a colonel who was commissioned from the ranks must retire at 55. A lieutenant-colonel who falls within the specialist field must retire at 55, and a major who falls in the specialist field must retire at the age of 55. These are the people who would be involved immediately if they are about to retire. Those who retire within the next five years will be doing so on a prorated basis.
Under Queen's Regulations and Orders Table A, article 1531, it is stated that a sergeant retires at age 50, and could have up to 30 years' service. In a case such as this, his indexing will accumulate for the next 10 years and he will get the lump sum increase at age 60 added to his pension.
Because of the earlier age that most military personnel are. required to retire, as opposed to those people in the public service and those who work for Crown corporations, it would be unfair to a service man if he had to wait until age 55 before his pension even started to become indexed. By that time he would be far behind those who retired at age 55 today. This is why indexing starts for him on the very day he retires. We get into the old argument with some saying we should be keeping these people in the armed forces longer because they are trained and still active, while others say we must keep a younger armed forces and these people must retire at certain ages. Even within the military community itself this is a debatable point.
Proposed section 4.1 of this measure on page 10 provides for a three-year review of pension funds by the chief actuary of the Department of Insurance, who will then report to the minister whether the pension fund is viable to meet the rate of inflation of the day. If the report is positive, the cabinet of the day has no choice but to allow full indexing in accordance with the viability of the fund. If in the opinion of the report the fund is not viable, then the governor in council sets the rate for the next three years. As has been said many times before, this bill prevents anyone from retiring very late in the year and getting the full indexing for the entire year. If a retiring person has the "85" formula and retires at the end of June he will receive the indexing for one half of that year, and similarly for other fractions of any one year.
In order to offset some of the innuendoes raised by the National Citizens' Coalition, it cannot be said often enough that approximately 85 per cent of today's retired public service personnel and armed forces personnel retired on a pension of less than $7,000 per year.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext: What was that figure?

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I said that 85 per cent retire on pensions of less than $7,000 per year. I put that figure on the record last fall when the former president of the treasury board made his introductory remarks. Therefore it is important that these people receive more supplementation than those in the much higher categories. You will recall that last fall full indexing would have been allowed on earnings up to that $7,000 mark, and above that the figure in the proposal was 8 per cent in 1979, 7 per cent for 1980, and 6 per cent in 1981. However, because this particular bill did not pass last year, this item will

come up for review once again and later this year we will find out whether the amount is going to be around $7,500, or somewhere around $8,000 for full indexing. These figures are very familiar to me as I have many neighbours who have retired from the armed forces or the public service and find themselves in this particular pension income bracket.
Even though this debate today is related to pensions in the public sector, I feel, Mr. Speaker, that there is a real need to take a good look at some of the private pension funds as well. Ministers of labour at the provincial levels and the federal Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) should discuss the problems faced by those who do not have a portable pension plan, in this day and age. In today's world, we find people in their 30's and early 40's by necessity moving around to find other jobs. In many cases a person might have 18 years with one company but, because he is laid off his job, or his position has become redundant, and he has to find another source of employment, he or she may lose that 18 years in the pension plan, and simply be given the amount he or she placed in the fund. Many of these pension plans fall under provincial jurisdiction, but our federal Minister of Labour, who is a very humanitarian type, could do a lot of good for private citizens across this country if he were to initiate such meetings with the provincial ministers of labour in order to provide portability of pension plans for every Canadian citizen across Canada who spent a reasonable amount of time working for one particular company and then found it necessary to move or, indeed, saw a chance for promotion in another area.
Again I wish to return to discuss a very serious problem that today faces many of our military personnel who retire at an early age. In many cases the trades that personnel in the armed forces practised for many years are not recognized once they arrive out on "civvy street". In many cases provincial departments of labour refuse to license mechanics, plumbers, carpenters and so on without further apprenticeship training. As a result they find themselves on the labour market with no qualifications of a legal nature but they do have the experience and knowledge of their field. I have had many people in my office discussing this very subject.
At the present time there is a military-civilian training accreditation committee working on this problem, but it still has a long way to go; even though it has made a very good start. In view of the considerable lapse of time between the time a member of the armed forces is pensioned off and the time he will reach 60 years of age for indexing, and under present conditions the age of 65 for the old age security, it becomes very necessary to provide him with a legal recognition of his skills so he can supplement his income during those crucial years.
In the United States forces, they quite often use the last year of a military person's career, if it is their wish to do so, to train them for a job when they get out of the service. I can only strongly recommend to the Minister of National Defence that this type of program be seriously looked at by the
February 14, 1979

Department of National Defence in Canada, and also that he might solicit the support of our good friend, the Minister of Labour, to deal with the provinces on civilian accreditation for the skills that members of the armed forces already have.
I wish to thank hon. members for their attention during my remarks. There are many other items I would like to discuss but I shall save them for committee stage.

speechtext: Flear, hear!

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on Bill C-12, legislation aimed essentially at reducing the level of benefits afforded to federal civil servants. Its main objective is to reduce the widening gap between public service and private sector pension funds. Pressured by representatives from the private sector, the government decided to reverse course on something that was apparently recognized for all civil servants, the indexing of their pensions.
As many of my colleagues in this House, I feel that pay differentials between the private and the public sectors are becoming a source of injustice. How many private sector workers toiled all their lives to get a meagre pension after 40 years? The government showed leadership when it put forward the indexing of retired public servants' pensions, and it believed the private sector would follow suit. We are now backing out, we are taking away full indexing from public servants and substituting this new system. A part only of pensions will now get automatic indexing. The minimum could be $7,500 or $8,000 a year, when some 80 per cent of pensioners are getting less than $7,000 a year.
Citizens once again will fall victim to this shortsighted government. By the same token bilingual public servants who had been promised the bilingualism supplement until 1983 were told last summer that would not be the case. Starting from April 1, they will stop getting it. And unemployment insurance claimants are now getting a maximum of $144 a week instead of $160, since January 1, 1979.
Mr. Speaker, the unemployed suffer a loss of revenue of some $16 a week, although a great number of them have obligations and often many dependents, with consumer prices on a constant increase. The Health Resources Fund schedule to end in 1980 was retroactively cancelled as of 1978, without consulting with the provinces.
The new provisions contained in this bill will cost between $38 million and $48 million less a year. This saving is very much in the spirit of the hatchet policy, as I call it, under which they cut expenses as much as possible without knowing exactly why and without too much concern for future consequences and especially for the people who are left in need. And all this is done to respond in one way or another to the industrial and financial lobbies.
Pensions
Mr. Speaker, I believe that all Canadians would support the government wholeheartedly if they were asked to cut down on their expenditures to have a healthier economy. Unfortunately, these drastic cutbacks will not improve the problems of unemployment and soaring price increases. Last summer, when he announced his decision to cut back expenditures, the right hon. Prime Minister said that this was the policy of the three r's which were restraint, renewal and reallocation. He was the only one to sing this tune. Indeed, he is still the only one. Everyone understood immediately what he meant by restraint, or budgetary restrictions. Indeed, we did not have long to wait for the axe to fall. Our unemployed know this better than anyone else because they were the first victims. But what concerns me most is that we still do not know when, how, why and where the other two r's, renewal and reallocation, will come in. We are still waiting. Nothing much has happened since then.
Bill C-60 made everyone unhappy and the Pepin-Robarts report will probably be left on the shelf since it does seem to please the Quebec premier a lot more than the Prime Minister of Canada. As for the reallocation concept, which was supposed to involve a reorientation of government funds towards employment programs, it seems to have been applied on a very small scale for a country which has more than 8 per cent of its manpower on unemployment, or nearly one million unemployed, and mostly among people. Where is the employment strategy that we have been demanding for many years? The unemployed are yelling at the top of their voice, but can the government hear them? The government is doing nothing, and that right before an election. What then will it do after the election?
The big problem resulting from the budgetary cuts, at least immediately it seems to me, is the decrease in the purchasing power of the citizens, whether they be retired or unemployed. Indeed, those steps will result unfortunately in reducing the standard of living of many citizens who will progressively become less and less able to buy consumer goods, the effects of which will be felt throughout the economic system, and that at a time when the Canadian dollar keeps sliding down.
Mr. Speaker, I am not criticizing the government for realizing that the gap between pension plans in the private sector and the public sector was leading, over the long term, to a completely unbalanced and inequitable situation. I am only insisting on the fact that the needs and hopes of civil servants were built up, and now the means of meeting them are being withdrawn. The public sector must not tag along behind the private sector. Instead, the gap between the two must simply be reduced to fairer proportions.
There is precious little awareness of the fact that budget cuts will have unfortunate socio-economic repercussions. I have repeatedly spoken-God knows how often-about adopt-

February 14, 1979
Pensions
ing the guaranteed annual income. Even the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) recognizes that such a program is desirable, though impossible at the present time. I say that a guaranteed annual income is not too heavy a load to bear when one considers the amounts already spent on unemployment insurance benefits and welfare. That would be a much fairer solution, a solution that would apply to the whole population and would not encourage disproportionate gaps, such as those we now know, between the public and the private sectors.
I wonder how much electioneering there is in this bill as we approach a federal election. Indeed in introducing this bill the government is trying to look good before bankers and financiers and part of the people. Those measures are only a first step toward the pure and simple abolition of escalation clauses in all federal plans. And, given those measures, private businesses will be very happy not to have to improve the escalation provisions in the pension plans of their own employees. Among other points of dispute between the government and civil servants, the principle of early retirement was mainly criticized. The civil servant who must retire involuntary because of a cutback in staff or his age cannot find another job and is helpless to fight inflation. There again, as always, private sector employees in the same position will face new restraints from the employers.
This bill starts from an entirely understandable purpose but uses means not likely to maintain harmonious relations in the public service. If the government backtracks too much on this, as it is doing with Bill C-12, the abolition of bilingual bonuses and the lay-offs of language teachers, we will soon have an explosive climate in the federal public service. That would be unfortunate because our public servants are competent and well organized.

Mr. Speaker, as I understand the situation I am the last speaker from this side of the House and this matter will be going to the committee shortly.
I want to reiterate on behalf of the official opposition, the Progressive Conservative party, that it is our intention to get this bill to committee as quickly as we can so that the examination that was spoken of so eloquently by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), in opening the debate for the official opposition, can continue. That kind of examination is absolutely essential in terms of this legislation.
The hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis), in the course of his speech the other evening, asked what the position of this party was with respect to the idea of pension indexing in the public service of Canada. He made some very flattering remarks about me, which I appreciate, and given the appropriate opportunity I will reciprocate. I do not like to quote myself, but in 1973 during the course of a debate I spoke on behalf of the Progressive Conservative party with respect to the position that was put before the House by the then president of the

treasury board. This was referred to by the then hon. member for York-Scarborough. The bill passed through all stages of the House within a few days. In fact I think second reading commenced on September 7 and it was back in the House on September 12, which was a very short period of time for a significant piece of legislation.
As you know, the amendment that was before us at that time respected full indexation on public service pensions, that is the range of the public service we speak of in the Public Service Superannuation Act. I said at that time:
Members of the government certainly are draftsmen of the bill, but if you examine the history of public service legislation you find that this government and its predecessors were really dragged, kicking and screaming, to the point where they finally gave in to what, over the years, were the reasonable demands of public service staff associations, the officers of public service associations, retired public servants and others who have written to people like myself and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
As I say, the government has finally given in and seen the reason for positions that have been taken by my party and, for that matter, the NDP with respect to this matter.
What happened on that occasion? Let us cast our minds back to that time. The president of the treasury board came into the House of Commons and indicated to us in a short, succinct statement that it was the intention of the Government of Canada to move in the direction of full indexation of pensions. He did not indicate to us in any way that there was any problem with respect to funding. He did not indicate in any way that we would be facing a bill in 1979 which changes the principles that were accepted by the House of Commons in 1973.
I believe the House of Commons and I at that time relied on a few things. First, I relied on the proposition that the president of the treasury board of that day knew what he was talking about. That may have been my first mistake. Second, I relied on the fact that behind that statement of the president of the treasury board there had been sufficient studies undertaken by the Government of Canada and they were prepared to come to the House with respect to that matter. That position was put by me on September 7, 1973, and later on September 12, 1973.
On third reading of the bill at page 6472 of Hansard I said this:
-it is my intention to be the only spokesman for my party at this final stage, and to expedite the passage of the measure.
That was the position put in 1973. With respect to the plight of people who are retired and who are no longer in the work force, people who cannot bargain for themselves, people who are subject to the ravages of inflation and other things, that has to remain the position. That must remain the principle that would guide any reasonable person looking upon individuals who may well be otherwise unprotected with respect to inflation. That is something I want to point out to the House. Why? Why is the principle of indexation relating pensions to the cost of living a reasonable one? It can be put in many ways.
I do not think it is appropriate in a reasonable society to adopt a position that people who cannot fend for themselves

ought to be left treading water in a stream which flows backward. That is akin to going downhill. I know the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Railton) is anxious to tell the House that he knows which way water flows, and I commend him for that.

I looked at the speech made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). In the course of his speech on this bill in the House on February 12, 1979, he said this:
I begin by saying I would be happy if the bill were not before us at all;-

The hon. member for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail) asks what is my position with respect to the National Citizens' Coalition. I will tell him my position. It has been a callous campaign, a campaign of half-truths. Hon. members will recall that it has been a campaign similar to that conducted on another occasion which brought disapprobation upon this House of Commons and its members. They have done exactly the same with the public service.
I would be the last one in the House to say that every public servant is not lazy, is not polite, and is not working his full share. There are public servants who tell me that there are others in the public service who are that way. For every one in the public service like that, it brings disapproval by the public. However, in general the public service of this country is reasonably good.
What public servants want is the opportunity to express themselves, to feel the challenge that others feel in various aspects of the community. There is nothing wrong with that. However, when I receive clippings from the National Citizens' Coalition I have to regard that as a result of some dishonest advocacy, something I flatly condemn.
There are some real changes to be made with regard to the public service. There ought to be a challenge for public servants. They should work to capacity. There should be changes in the bargaining procedures and a whole host of things that affect public servants. The cause of a public service and its respect for itself are not advanced in any way by the kind of attack that has been made by the National Citizens' Coalition. It is a matter of prejudicial guesswork at best, and I am being lenient when I call it that.
The hon. member for Restigouche wants to know my position. I will tell him. A public servant has told me directly what he thinks about the national coalition. This is what he said:
Dear Sirs:
I'm mad as hell about this type of misrepresentation with respect to the public service indexed pension-civil servants indexed pensions.
He went on to add, and I commend this to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien):
-and government use of my pension contributions at ridiculously low interest rates.
The Minister of Finance might want to take that message to heart when considering this matter. Other speakers in the debate have pointed out the questions that should be asked in committee and the inquiries that should be made. The hon. member for Hamilton West did a service by laying out those questions.
This House should never again fall into the trap of accepting what this government says about anything. The government has in effect said that this is the best it can do. We must examine that. There is a difference of opinion in this House. In fact there is a difference of opinion on the government side as to whether this is the best it can do.
I suggest that hon. members reread the speech of the hon. member for Ottawa West. If the figures that he gave are true,

On the other hand, if the position of the President of the Treasury Board is correct and we have to change the law so that we fully index for 85 per cent of members of the public service who retire, then his predecessor, the Hon. C. M. Drury, when speaking in this House in 1973 misled this House, the public service, and the people of Canada. That is why we need to have this kind of examination. We can no longer accept at face value what the government says.
We have to examine ourselves with regard to how we feel on these principles. We must ask ourselves whether this bill is fair and proper in light of circumstances revealed at that committee, and given the difference of opinion with regard to changing the law and therefore the benefits. Eighty-five per cent is not a bad batting average for any government. I concede that. That is one of the reasons we will send this bill to committee.
Yesterday I received a call from someone who will be just outside the 85 per cent, just above the $8,500 figure with regard to his pension. The other evening the President of the Treasury Board was optimistic enough to say that indexing may go up to $8,000 or $8,500 on the fully indexed portion. This man is just above that. I cannot bury a constituent in statistics any more than 1 can bury an old age security recipient in statistics and advocate a means test for OAS. Nobody on the other side will do that, and I hope nobody expects us to do it. That is why we must examine what the hon. member for Ottawa West says to see whether there is an embarrassment of riches in that plan, whether the bill is really necessary, and whether the level of benefits should fall. That is the examination which is to take place. That is the position taken by the hon. member for Hamilton West. We are entitled to these answers. The public service is entitled to these answers.
It is important that we do not follow with respect to this bill a process of perfunctory consideration and quick passage through committee. It is important that public service organizations, and those outside the public service as well, should have an opportunity to give evidence before the committee. It is important that what happens in the committee is not a repetition of what happens in committees from time to time when full examination is not allowed. We cannot get to the truth completely in the House of Commons even though members do their best; everyone knows that the major work of parliament is not done here but in committee where matters can be pursued in detail.
I have another cautionary word to add. It may be satisfactory that we can accept that things look pretty good for the next biennial period, and, who knows, that they may well look good for the triennial period after that. I hope this is the case. But we are not really looking to the next triennial period, we are talking about a succession of other triennial periods down the path. I don't think we can grasp this bill to our bosoms and

accept it as the last word. We have to understand that we are not looking just to the next election or beyond the next three years or the triennial period after that. We are looking well into the future. What we are doing here affects the situation and the future of very large numbers of people.
We are prepared to accept this bill today provided there is to be the careful examination of which I have spoken. I am not prepared to fall gratefully into the arms of the government with respect to this measure. As far as the government is concerned, I am from Missouri; I have got to be shown. I have joined the host of Canadians-or they have joined me-who feel the government has mishandled the economic situation. The House of Commons, on behalf of the public we serve and on behalf of the public service, which is part of our responsibility, should examine this plan so that we are not required to go through this kind of exercise again.
I want to say something, now, with respect to the future of this country. A number of people have made known their views with regard to that future in terms of pension payments and the way in which governments at various levels are able to consider at least providing "hedges" in pension plans for their retired workers. There has been a great outburst in the community because it is felt that similar provisions are not possible on the private side. That is a matter of debate. It is a question we all have to ask ourselves as public men and women, people who are here for a time to represent others, to represent the community. We have to be prepared to assess the truth of these assertions-to consider whether it is, in fact, impossible. If we do not examine them there are others in the community who will do so.
Is it the case that in a country as rich as ours, with a population as ingenious as ours, with corporations whose leaders are as ingenious as they are, that it can be said without doubt that we are not capable of devising ways in which those who are not relying on public sector pensions and who are relying to a large degree on private sector pensions can find some ways to build into their pensions provision against the ravages of inflation? I might point out that this would not be necessary if governments could control inflation. This is a situation which places a tremendous onus on governments everywhere. That is the bottom line in the pension business. If inflation is contained to a small amount the argument about indexation loses its force.
If people outside the work force face the inflation which can be called ravaging inflation-those are the words which have been used to describe inflation as it affects those people today-and if they are relying to a great extent on pension plans which are not related in some way to the cost of living, then the fact is that those people are falling further and further behind. I believe it was the hon. member for Ottawa West-someone did-who put some figures on the record in this debate with respect to the fact that our population is aging. The aging constituency of all of us in this House is growing. The sheer political power of that constituency is growing. As it grows, its voice within the country will grow along with it. That constituency will put upon us a responsibility which we may not be prepared to look at now, but a responsibility will be put on us and others like us to protect those who are less fortunate in that broad economic sense because they are not in the work force. That is something with which we will all have to deal.
I think it is important that this debate be conducted in that atmosphere. Let us face the fact that those in that constituen-
Pensions
cy face a major problem. Let us not think that the critics of indexation are able to silence the debate in the country merely by saying that as far as they are concerned it does not exist and that they will not look at it. That debate is going to go on in this country. It is being carried on now. It has been carried on, and if hon. members have not read it, I commend to them the brief which was filed before the Royal Commission on the Status of Pensions in Ontario by Eckler, Brown, Segal and Company Limited, in which this question was addressed and in which the question of costs was addressed. We will eventually have to address this matter.
I also commend to hon. members an article published in 1979 in papers on "Canadian Public Policy" by Professor James E. Pesando of the Institute for Policy Analysis of the University of Toronto, because he addresses the question of the ability of the private sector to maintain itself in times of inflation. He argues that indexing is a feasible although challenging objective. He had something to say about the Tomen-son-Alexander report, which I think should be taken with an appropriate grain of salt and subject to examination by the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
Professor Pesando said this, and I am quoting from page 84 of the article:
To sum up, the procedures employed by Tomenson-Alexander have the effect of artificially (and, ultimately, arbitrarily) reducing the liabilities in respect to the real benefits and increasing those in respect to the indexing provisions by an equivalent amount. This result is of crucial importance if the cost of the indexing provisions as identified by Tomenson-Alexander is used as an argument against the indexing of private pensions.
I hope the two representations to which I have referred will be considered by the committee because we have to consider this bill while recognizing the realities of Canadian society. I cannot believe that the pension industry in Canada, which is reasonably and appropriately led by men of wisdom and business acumen, despite their reluctance to address the problem-and there is some reluctance-is in fact not looking at the problem. I suspect that over the next ten or 15 years as the clamour develops, whether we like it, whether they like it, or whether anyone likes it, we will be driven to consider how this can be accomplished and, in its accomplishment, what the role of the government will be in this undertaking.
In the context of this debate I do not think we can forget that there is editorial opinion. It may be wrong. I do not know. Within the last year or two an opinion was expressed in an editorial which appeared in a newspaper in the United Kingdom. That editorial commented on a speech made by the head of the United Kingdom Actuarial Society. In that speech it was stated that we must regard pensions less as an actuarial problem and more as an economic problem, and that we ought to look more at the ability of a country to bear the pension burden, and examine it from that point of view.
If we do not get inflation under control in this country, I suggest that we will not be able to withstand the pressure applied by those who find themselves exposed more greatly than they are today and who will come to legislatures for remedies. That is a long-term issue from which this parliament and succeeding parliaments cannot turn away. What will these
