that Bill C-37, to amend the statute law relating to income tax, to amend the Canada Pension Plan and to provide other authority for the raising of funds, be read the second time and referred to Committee of the Whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill, together with the bill to amend the Excise Tax Act, implements my budget measures. The major objectives of those measures are, first, to maintain and accelerate growth in demand through fiscal stimulus; second, at the same time to put downward pressure on prices and costs in order to protect our renewed competitive position; third, to provide further stimulus to capital spending and research and development so as to improve industrial productivity and efficiency and to ensure continued growth; fourth, to assist particular sectors in overcoming structural problems;
Income Tax
fifth, to provide more support for regional development; and sixth, to take action to maintain the integrity of Canada's tax system. My budget has been described as a responsible budget. The tax measures before us implement the budget objectives in a responsible way.
The bill reduces taxes for working individuals. It does this by doubling the limit for the employment expense deduction, increasing it from $250 to $500 a year. Being related to employment income, this measure provides additional incentive and reward for working Canadians. It will reduce federal and provincial tax by some $365 million in the 1979-80 fiscal year.
But this is not the only element acting to spur growth in disposable incomes of Canadians in 1979. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that tax indexing will result in a $1.6 billion reduction in federal and provincial income taxes. I also announced a reduction in the contribution rate for unemployment insurance. I have reduced the federal sales tax from 12 per cent to 9 per cent, thus boosting purchasing power by about $1 billion. For a married family earning the average industrial wage, these measures taken altogether should raise real after-tax disposable income by over two and a half per cent. Canadians will pay a lower share of their total income in taxes in 1979 than they did in 1978. The stimulus provided by these measures will support consumption demand over the coming months. As well, strong stimulatory forces are at work as a result of a more competitive dollar. More demand means more capacity utilization and more incentive to investment.
I would like to refer to two other tax changes affecting individuals. They are not as large as those I have just mentioned but, in their own way, are just as important. Hon. members will recall the concern expressed at the time of the last budget over the taxation of RRSPs in cases where both parents die leaving minor or disabled children. I have found that this is a valid concern. This bill provides that, in these cases, specified amounts may pass to dependent children or grandchildren without being taxed in the hands of the deceased. The amounts will qualify for forward averaging for tax purposes in the hands of the children. The allowable amounts are larger for younger children than for older ones, with a maximum of $125,000. In the case of disabled children, the limit is a flat $125,000 regardless of age. The tax benefits from this can amount to tens of thousands of dollars. This bill also includes provisions to permit those who are disabled or whose spouse is disabled to mature their RRSP funds before they reach age 60. Such persons will now be able to purchase an annuity or an RRIF at any time.
'
A strong industrial structure is vital to Canada's future. A more efficient industrial structure means lower costs and increased competitiveness. The government has put in place a large number of tax measures to spur industrial development, to help particular sectors, and to promote activities which are of importance to industry. Hon. members are familiar with the two-year write-off and low federal tax rate on manufacturing. The budget papers indicate that, as a result of these measures,

February 14, 1979
Income Tax
corporate income tax on Canadian manufacturing as a per cent of profits is some 10 per cent lower than is the case in the United States. The federal tax incentives for mining result in a preferential federal tax environment. Past budgets have provided tax incentives which make investments in research and development much more attractive. These are but a few examples of the many ways the tax system plays a role in economic development and support.
Prior to formulating my budget I talked with representatives of many sectors. The recommendations of the sectoral task forces were thoroughly reviewed within my department. 1 benefited greatly from these efforts. Many of the sectoral task forces made recommendations concerning the investment tax credit. I have responded to those recommendations. This bill provides an indefinite extension of the federal tax credit past June, 1980. Now business will be able to plan and develop even their largest projects in an orderly fashion. Moreover, the measure will give them benefits amounting to $500 million for investments made after June, 1980.
This bill also enriches the tax credit. The basic rate of credit will be increased from 5 per cent to 7 per cent. Also other rates are increased. The benefits from the increased rates of credit apply from November 16, 1978.
These changes to the investment credit promote investment in some very important sectors. The benefits go to manufacturing and processing businesses, the petroleum and mineral industries, logging, farming, fishing and grain storage. As a result of the extension and enrichment of the investment tax credit, I look to measurable improvements in Canada's productive capacity, better growth, productivity and cost performance over the medium term.
Provisions of this bill extend the 7 per cent credit to apply to long-haul transportation equipment. Items such as aircraft, inter-city buses, long-haul trucks and trailers, vessels and railway rolling stock, track grading and other equipment will qualify. The tax benefits involved amount to about $30 million annually. Canada's transportation system is one of the sinews of the country. It will be stronger and more efficient as a result. Efficiency will mean lower costs. Also this measure will promote better services to passengers, with more modern equipment.
Regional development is a cornerstone of Canada's structural economic policies. Regional development grants are a prime example of our commitment. Fiscal equalization has long been a part of federal-provincial financial arrangements. The equalization program will provide some $2.6 billion to qualifying provinces in this fiscal year.
We have used the tax system to foster a better distribution of economic activity across Canada's regions. This bill adds to the regional tax incentives already in place. It doubles the investment tax credit in the Maritimes and Gaspe from 10 per cent to 20 per cent. This is equivalent in its effects to a cost reduction of 20 per cent of the price of eligible machinery, equipment and structures used in these areas. In other desig-

nated areas the credit rises from 7.5 per cent to 10 per cent. These areas cover most of Quebec outside the Gaspe, northern Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, parts of northern British Columbia and northern Alberta, as well as the Yukon and Northwest Territories. While it would be wrong to expect immediate results, I believe this type of distinction by region can lead to significant improvements in economic potential over time.
Also I should like to emphasize that these regionalized credit rates strongly support our sectoral policies. Mining and pulp and paper, two of the sectors toward which my budget was directed, both will benefit generally from the higher credit rates of 10 per cent and 20 per cent. As a result of the enrichment of the investment tax credit and its indefinite extension, the private sector will earn over $1 billion in benefits in respect of their investment in the first full year in which the changes are in effect. Some $500 million will be claimable immediately in the year while the remainder, mostly representing credit earned by non-taxable firms, will be carried forward to reduce tax in subsequent years.
Let me turn to research and development. Over the recent past the government has taken a range of substantial tax actions to promote R and D. Adequate incentives for R and D have been stressed by the sectoral task forces and others. Canada must ensure a first class R and D effort. More R and D in Canadian industry is essential for good economic performance over the medium term. This government is committed to doing its part to achieve this goal through a variety of measures including tax incentives, direct grants and subsidies. The bill adds to the support already in place. The basic investment tax credit for R and D now will be doubled. It will be higher than for other investments. Since 1977 the after-tax cost of R and D has fallen by half. This is a result of measures taken by me and my predecessors.
While it is too early to evaluate the full effects of these measures, preliminary indications are that firms are showing interest. They are looking to stepping up their R and D effort. Some firms which have not made a commitment to R and D are starting to do so.
I want to direct Your Honour's attention for a moment to R and D of small firms. It is a matter which has been raised in the House before. Unfortunately small firms do not themselves engage in an adequate amount of R and D. For the health of the future Canadian economy they must be encouraged to do so. This bill addresses that problem directly. It contains an R and D credit of 25 per cent for small firms. It is the richest of any tax credit applying to investment. I know of no analogous measure in another industrialized country. What matters for ensuring improved R and D performance is that R and D be made more attractive relative to other investments the firm might undertake. It is noteworthy, therefore, that for small manufacturing firms the relative cost advantage in favour of R and D over other investments is greater than is the case for large firms.
February 14, 1979

As a result of these measures the after-tax cost of R and D can be as low as 15 cents in several provinces. This is without taking into account any grants that may also be available. The R and D tax measures will provide a tax reduction of $100 million over and above the value of the immediate fast writeoff for R and D that has been in place for some time. Several of the measures also reduce provincial taxes. Successful R and D has a high rate of return, higher than many other investments. Research and development is, however, risky. I believe that these tax incentives ensure that the risk does not lead to underinvestment. They produce a tax environment that is very favourable to attaining Canada's R and D goals.
This bill contains other tax cuts to aid important sectors of the economy. I turn first to resource taxation, and mining in particular. Federal and provincial ministers have finished a review of mining taxation. Let me say in passing that this review, in my opinion, represents a prime example of the kind of co-operation the Canadian federation can and should accommodate. The review report makes instructive reading, and I commend it to hon. members.
As I said in my budget, the report shows that the federal tax system is basically sound. In 1975, the latest year for which actual data are available, the federal tax was only some 14.4 per cent of industry profits. In the same year the federal tax rate on manufacturing was 23.6 per cent, which itself was a preferential rate compared with other industries. Under the federal system, no tax is generally payable on new mine investments until capital is recovered.
The federal share of total government revenue from mining is only some 33 per cent. This compares with our share of over-all corporate income tax from all sectors of some 70 per cent. And the federal share of revenues from mining has been declining. I do not believe, therefore, that an unbiased observer would claim that the onus was on the federal government to reduce its taxes dramatically even if further tax reductions are in order.
Nonetheless, I did decide, in framing my budget, that some additional incentives for new mine development were warranted, and I wanted to provide leadership to the provinces in this matter. Accordingly, this bill contains three major changes affecting mining. First, development expenditures will now be written off at 100 per cent immediately. Second, townsite and other social capital expenditures at new mine sites will earn the depletion deduction of one third of their cost. Third, mining will be a major beneficiary of the investment tax credit and of the indefinite extension of the pollution abatement incentive. The total value of all of these measures to mining is some $60 million per year.
I am pleased that I was able to take the lead in acting upon the principles put forward in the resource taxation report. While I, of course, cannot be sure, I expect and hope that provinces will take up this lead. I want to reiterate that the federal government will pursue the spirit of co-operation established during the review. This government will seek to avoid tax system changes that create undue uncertainty, and it will
Income Tax
not take tax action to offset the benefits from any tax reductions that provinces introduce.
There are other measures in the budget directed to particular sectors. In oil and gas this bill provides for continuation of drilling fund incentives. They have been very successful. The amount of funds going into exploration and development m oil and gas annually, through these funds, has grown from nothing to up to $500 million currently. As a result of the extension of the measure a continued high level of exploration activity will be encouraged.
The pulp and paper industry will receive significant tax benefits over the coming years from the extension of the two-year write-off for pollution abatement equipment. This will be accomplished by changes to the income tax regulations. Reducing pollution is an important goal. This measure acts to lessen costs to industry of installing pollution abatement equipment. The pulp and paper industry will also benefit from the enhanced investment tax credit. The credit applies to pollution abatement investments as well as other investments in this sector.
Housing is benefited by extension of the preferential tax treatment of multiple unit residential buildings. It also benefits from the reinstatement of deductibility of interest on property taxes on land awaiting development. Conditions in the housing market are different than in 1974 when this deductibility was denied, and it is time to reinstate it.

Mr. Speaker, the bill under study includes important amendments which will affect businesses. The amendments I already referred to would reduce corporate taxes. Others, would have the effect of amending our tax legislation according to the development of our economy. They would allow us to make sure that federal taxes will remain fair and equitable for all Canadian taxpayers. One of the main responsibilities of a finance minister is to make sure that the taxation system will remain equitable. Bill C-37 would allow us to achieve that goal. In that context, I would like to have a look at the provisions of the bill which are related to income bonds and term preferred shares. Traditionally any income originating from such shares was considered as dividend. That was the practice, without taking into account that those shares were actually proofs of debts. It made some sense in the case of some businesses which used those shares, more precisely income bonds, when they were facing serious financial difficulties.
As a matter of fact, this is why income bonds were created in 1930. But now, this form of financing is used mainly by multinational or national companies which are in a sound financial position. For some borrowers, the fact that the financing costs are in the form of non-deductible dividends does not matter very much. Some have more tax incentives than necessary to ensure that they have no tax to pay, whatever happens. Their non taxable situation does not mean that they are in a difficult financial position.

February 14, 1979
Income Tax
This type of financing attracts industrial lenders because their investment income in the form of dividends is not taxable. In fact this financing system means that tax incentives which are not claimed by industrial firms can be used to reduce the tax which would otherwise be payable by banks and other financial institutions. Of course there would be no problem if the amounts were small. If the funds were going into productive investments, there would be no great difficulty, but such is not the case. Chartered bank assets in the form of income bonds or debentures and term preferred shares in the 12 months ended October 1978 went from $3 billion to $7.2 billion.
I have indicated that Canadian government and provincial revenues are eroded to the tune of some $500 million a year. Because of this, the tax rate on bank earnings plummeted from 40 per cent to some 30 per cent. Tax revenue from bank earnings remained roughly constant from 1977 to 1978, although their profits increased some 20 per cent. Further, a significant part of those funds did not go into new productive investments. Takeovers were thus made easier. Those funds were used to re-finance existing standard loans in order to derive maximum benefits from fiscal savings. In the period ending October 1978, the volume of that type of securities in bank portfolios increased tremendously. Also, most of their total assets used in any form of industrial financing were settled.
I could not let the situation go on. This legislation therefore provides that the revenue from shares issued after budget night will be taxed the same way as interest revenue. Revenue from that source will be taxable when received by banks and other lenders. The new issues of term preferred shares with a term higher than 10 years are more in the nature of shares than loans. For this reason they will not be affected. Borrowers facing financial difficulties will still be entitled to existing fiscal status.
I would now turn to the second major initiative of a structural nature involving the corporate tax structure. It concerns the reduced tax rate available to small businesses. As I indicated in my budget, Mr. Speaker, small businesses are afforded very generous tax provisions. This is mainly due to the lower tax rate available to those companies and the dividend. A businessman who is incorporated and earns $50,000 pays in fact $4,000 to $5,000 less in federal and provincial tax than as a wage earner or as a professional who is not incorporated, at this salary level.
The fiscal benefits of incorporation are greater at the top of the income scale. It is to the advantage of the businessman whose small business is incorporated because he can save by not distributing his business income. The income tax rate is only 20 or 25 per cent. Any additional tax payable on personal

income is deferred until the businessman distributes the undistributed income. In the meantime the taxation rate for personal income tax may be less. Individuals can save on an income which is sometimes subject to much higher rates of taxation, and the opportunities for tax returns are much more limited.
The lesser taxation rate for corporations represents a reduction of $900 million a year in corporate income tax. There is an annual tax saving of $5,000 per corporation. In addition to these measures, shareholders of small companies are subject to a special tax system as regards capital gains. The study I have published and which compares the Canadian and American tax systems clearly illustrates that our tax system is much more advantageous to the small businessman.
Mr. Speaker, I firmly believe that we are justified, through our tax system, in favouring small business as such. It needs this edge to cope in the business world and with economic risks, to get the necessary capital for growth and job creation, as well as to be able to compete with larger Canadian and foreign firms.
On the other hand, I do not believe that these tax privileges must extend to activities where the characteristics of small businesses cannot be taken into account. By allowing this we would simply increase the fiscal burden of everyone else and cause a general lack of respect for the fairness of the taxation system. In this regard, certain situations in the past have caused serious problems.
Members of professional classes in certain provinces can form a corporation or a company, but they cannot do so in others. This does not provide for fairness. For instance, in the past a doctor or a lawyer living in a province where the members of this profession can form a corporation or a company paid much less federal income tax than another member of the same profession in another province. On principle, I do not believe that the provincial legislation governing incorporation should cause such major differences in the amount of federal income tax payable.
In the provinces where the members of a profession cannot incorporate, they set up management companies whose only aim was to siphon off professional income or fees as administrative, management or financial services. This income could then entitle them to the reduced taxation rate. Such management companies often belonged to the wife of a man in a professional class. Thus, the benefits of the reduced taxation rate provided for small businesses were added to those of income sharing.
The financial situation of professional classes is not the same as that of the small business. Their income is much more stable. Access to these professions is justifiably carefully controlled. The deduction offered to small businesses was implemented when incorporation by professional classes did not constitute a problem. This deduction was never aimed at providing these people with a privileged taxation status.
February 14, 1979

Other workers, such as managers, have begun to incorporate to take advantage of the reduced taxation rate. Court rulings have also entitled investment and rental income to this reduced rate. As I said in my budget speech, it would be unfair to allow such practices to go on because in so doing, Mr. Speaker, we are in fact imposing a heavier tax burden on those who are not incorporated.
The provisions of the bill and the draft regulations that accompany it are aimed at four types of businesses: first, doctors, dentists, lawyers and accountants; second, businesses set up to offer managerial, financial, administrative or similar services to an associate company; third, businesses set up to manage the investment portfolio of an individual; fourth, the employee who incorporates himself. The details that apply will be found in the draft regulations I have had published. I am still receiving useful observations with regard to the specifics of those regulations. I promise to examine any question submitted to me by hon. members in the course of this debate. 1 shall put the finishing touches to the regulations in light of all the comments I shall have received.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention four specific points to hon. members: first, those provisions do not alter in any way the right to incorporate when there are valid reasons to do so and when provincial laws allow it. I expect that some members of the professions, management businesses and others will continue to incorporate. Second, the provisions stipulate the same rate of income tax for all groups concerned, as is the case in a good many other businesses: no more, no less. Finally, those who are already incorporated can, in many cases, see to it that their income tax is no higher than if they were not incorporated and received their income directly.
Third, my measures provide small incorporated businesses with a privileged fiscal system when compared to what exists in the United States where incorporation provides much fewer tax advantages. They have nothing comparable to our dividend tax credit. It is therefore impossible in the United States to pay less tax by having the income pass through a business instead of getting it directly. There are tax fines levied on income from professional service businesses and personal assets businesses. Therefore, the U.S. tax system tends to discourage the practice of deferring income tax by not distributing funds. Fourth, those measures concern more than a few of the 300,000 small incorporated businesses eligible for the reduced tax rate.
Businesses in the manufacturing, processing, construction, agriculture, fisheries, resource mining and development, wholesale and retail trade sectors continue to benefit from the provisions for small businesses. It will be the same for nearly all businesses in the service industries, including hotels, motels, businesses providing personal, particular or teaching services, driving schools and general insurance agencies.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, this bill requests a borrowing authority of some $10 billion for fiscal year 1979-80. Hon. members
Income Tax
will recall that in November, 1978 additional authority for $7 billion was granted. Most borrowing authorities obtained before November, 1978 have been used, except for a part that remains available for the next fiscal or subsequent years. Any unused amount of the $7 billion borrowing authority granted last November will be cancelled on March 31, 1979.
We anticipate for 1979-80 cash requirements of some $10,750 million, excluding exchange rates. The borrowing authority requested at this time should be enough to meet our cash requirements and a margin for contingencies like foreign borrowings. The government is expected to begin fiscal 197980 with rather high cash balances part of which could be used to meet cash requirements.
All unused borrowing authorities provided for in this new legislation for 1979-80 in respect of which the governor in council has not taken any action will be cancelled on March 31, 1980, under section 37 of the Financial Administration Act. Mr. Speaker, those are the remarks I wanted to make in introducing this bill which flows from my budget.
I was not in the House yesterday when I was blamed for being absent. I want to apologize to the House-
If I was not here it was because I had a long standing engagement to make a speech in New York before an important forum. Suddenly yesterday the opposition decided that it was a good time to have a motion. This motion could have been debated during other opposition days earlier on. In any event I was working in New York yesterday, and today I was speaking in Quebec. I have not had time to read the speeches and comments that were made in my absence. Questions were asked yesterday. By the way, I would be glad, Mr. Speaker, if you would stop me at this point. If you can guarantee that during the debate on this budget bill, no one will speak about the dollar, I will shut up right away.

Relating to the level of the deficit, people on the other side are always talking about the deficit of this government and saying that the debt level is so fantastically high. I would like to tell hon. members that in 1962 under the last Conservative government-and I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was here at that time-the public debt in Canada was 33.4 per cent of the gross national product, and today it is only 18.9 per cent.

Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition and members of the opposition, during the course of asking bright questions but not offering any solutions, asked why I was not going to the IMF. It is very simple. One goes to the IMF when one is broke. Canada's credit is good. We can go to Germany, Japan and the United States any day for credit. Yesterday I was in New York and I could have borrowed $1 billion just like that. So I am not going to the IMF, and for a very good reason. When one is forced to go to the IMF it is because there is no more credit available. As well, if one goes to the IMF, the IMF will then run the country for you more or less, because they set down the guidelines. If we can go on the open market and borrow money, it is because Canada's credit is pretty good. If the Leader of the Opposition did not know that, I will tell him today.
The professor from Don Valley asked why we do not force the Bank of Canada to reduce its secondary reserves. We could do that. However, what would be the effect? The effect would be to push the interest rates higher. It would reduce the money supply in Canada. That is the same member who got up and complained about the high level of interest rates in Canada.
I would like the public to reflect on the policies they propose. I could give the whole list, one after the other. They are laughable. There will be other occasions for that. Tomorrow I will be before the committee.

We have been the government lately. Some say too long. We have helped to escalate development of the tar sands. We have given great incentives so that exploration for oil and gas will be carried out in the north and in the Beaufort Sea.
When I see the troubled world in which we live today, I see that we are a very fortunate people. Of course this country is not perfect. After all, we are all human beings. But Canadians do not realize how fortunate we are.
Some say we do not have good economic policies in Canada.
I was privileged to be in Argentina on a business trip during the recess. I was amazed at what I was told by the minister of finance of that country. He told me that right after the war Canada and Argentina were equal in terms of population, GNP, resources, and potential. We have followed two different courses. They became extremely nationalist, protectionist, and intervened a lot. We did not. We became the traders of the world. Per capita, we are the biggest trading nation in the world, almost $100 billion of trade both ways, export and import, and a gross national product of $250 billion. They followed the course of closing their borders, intervening in efficient industries, and becoming protectionist.
Look at the results after 30 years. Our GNP in American dollars is about $220 billion. Theirs is about one fifth of that. We buy and sell about $85 billion U.S. every year. Argentina buys and sells on the international market about $10 billion or $11 billion. Our figure is eight times as much because we have followed the course of an open society in trading with the world with no exchange controls, importing and exporting capital and dealing with all nations of the world. When I hear all the gloom and doom speeches, I think there is nothing better than what we have here.
